title: Salicylic vs Glycolic vs TCA: Choosing the Right Peel for Your Skin
meta_description: How salicylic, glycolic and TCA peels differ, which skin concern each suits best, and how to choose the right peel for Indian skin — a dermatologist's guide.
image_alt: Chemical peel solution and an applicator brush on a clinic treatment tray, illustrating the choice between salicylic, glycolic and TCA peels

quick_facts.label: Salicylic (BHA)
quick_facts.value: Oil-loving — best for oily, acne-prone and congested skin and blackheads. Anti-inflammatory and comedolytic.

quick_facts.label: Glycolic (AHA)
quick_facts.value: Water-loving — best for dullness, texture, fine lines and epidermal pigmentation. The best-studied for melasma on Indian skin.

quick_facts.label: Mandelic (AHA)
quick_facts.value: A larger, gentler AHA — favoured for darker and sensitive skin and melasma, with a lower irritation and pigmentation risk.

quick_facts.label: TCA
quick_facts.value: Stronger and can go deeper — for texture, deeper pigment and scars, but used cautiously on Indian skin due to pigmentation risk.

quick_facts.label: The real answer
quick_facts.value: There's no single 'best' peel — the right one depends on your concern, skin type and tone, which is why a clinician matches it to you.

intro:
Walk into any conversation about chemical peels and you'll hear the same names — salicylic, glycolic, mandelic, TCA — usually with someone insisting one is 'the best'. The truth is that none of them is universally best; they're different tools for different jobs, and the right choice depends on what you're treating, your skin type and, on Indian skin especially, your tolerance for pigmentation risk. A salicylic peel is excellent for one person and the wrong choice for another.

This guide breaks down how the main peeling agents actually differ — chemically and in what they do — and matches each to the concerns it suits best, so you understand the logic behind the peel your clinician recommends rather than chasing a name you read online. We'll cover salicylic, glycolic, mandelic and TCA, what the evidence says about them, and the special considerations for choosing a peel on darker Indian skin.

sections.heading: AHA vs BHA: The Fundamental Split
sections.html:
The first and most useful distinction is between AHAs (alpha-hydroxy acids) and BHAs (beta-hydroxy acids), and it comes down to one property: whether the acid is water-loving or oil-loving. Glycolic, lactic and mandelic acids are AHAs — they're water-soluble, work mainly on the skin's surface, and excel at exfoliating dead cells, smoothing texture, brightening dullness and improving epidermal pigmentation. They're the 'glow and tone' acids.

Salicylic acid is the classic BHA — it's oil-soluble, which means it can penetrate into oily, sebum-filled pores and dissolve the debris inside them. That makes it the 'congestion and acne' acid: it gets into pores where water-based AHAs can't, and it's also anti-inflammatory. So the very first sorting question for choosing a peel is: is your main problem on the surface (dullness, texture, tone → AHA) or in the pores (oiliness, blackheads, acne → BHA)? Many people have both, which is why blended and alternating approaches exist — but understanding this split explains most of why a clinician reaches for one acid over another.

sections.heading: Salicylic Acid: For Oily, Acne-Prone, Congested Skin
sections.html:
Salicylic acid is the go-to peel for oily and acne-prone skin, blackheads, whiteheads and congestion. Because it's oil-soluble it penetrates into the pore, clearing the sebum and dead-cell plugs that drive comedonal acne, and it calms inflammation. According to PubMed, a randomised controlled trial found that a course of 30% salicylic acid peels produced significant improvement in moderate-to-severe acne, and a large Cochrane review of topical acne treatments places salicylic acid among the agents used for acne. It's also useful for the post-acne marks that acne leaves behind, treating cause and consequence together.

Salicylic peels are generally well tolerated and relatively low-downtime, and they suit the thicker, oilier skin common in humid Indian conditions. Who it's not ideal for: very dry or sensitive skin (it can be drying), and it's not the first choice if your main concern is deep lines or dermal pigmentation rather than oil and congestion. There's also a true (if rare) salicylate allergy to be aware of. For the right candidate — oily, congested, breakout-prone skin — it's often the single most satisfying peel.

sections.heading: Glycolic Acid: For Dullness, Texture and Pigmentation
sections.html:
Glycolic acid is the most widely used and best-studied AHA, and the smallest AHA molecule, so it penetrates readily and works efficiently on the surface. It's the peel of choice for dullness, uneven texture, fine lines and epidermal pigmentation, exfoliating and speeding turnover to reveal brighter, smoother skin, and with repeated use stimulating some collagen. On Indian skin it has the strongest evidence for pigmentation: according to PubMed, glycolic acid facial peels improved melasma in 91% of Indian women in one study, with epidermal-type melasma responding best, and no significant side effects when done with proper priming and sun protection.

Because glycolic penetrates quickly, its strength and contact time are adjusted carefully — a higher-percentage glycolic peel left on too long can irritate and, on darker skin, risk pigmentation, so it's titrated to your skin. It pairs well with other treatments (for acne scars, an RCT combined microneedling with a glycolic peel to good effect). Who it's less ideal for: very oily, congestion-dominant skin may do better with salicylic, and very reactive skin may do better with mandelic. For most people wanting brighter, smoother, more even skin, glycolic is the versatile workhorse.

sections.heading: Mandelic Acid: The Gentle AHA for Darker and Sensitive Skin
sections.html:
Mandelic acid deserves its own section because it's often the smartest choice for Indian skin, even though it gets less attention than glycolic. It's an AHA, but its molecule is much larger than glycolic's, so it penetrates more slowly and evenly. That slower penetration translates into less irritation and a lower risk of post-inflammatory pigmentation — exactly the complication darker skin is prone to — while still delivering brightening, mild exfoliation and help with pigmentation and mild acne.

For these reasons many dermatologists favour mandelic acid (alone or blended) for Fitzpatrick IV–VI skin, sensitive skin, melasma and first-time peelers, where glycolic might be more irritating. The trade-off is that, being gentler, it can be a little less dramatic per session than a stronger glycolic peel, so results build over a course. A Cochrane review noted a salicylic-mandelic combination peel performed comparably to a glycolic peel for acne, reflecting how useful these gentler and blended options are. If your skin is deep-toned, sensitive, or you've reacted badly to peels before, mandelic is well worth asking about — it's the 'all the benefit, less of the risk' option for Indian skin. Our dedicated guide on mandelic acid for Indian skin covers it in depth.

sections.heading: TCA: Stronger, Deeper — and Used with Caution
sections.html:
Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a different class of peeling agent — not an AHA or BHA, but a stronger acid that, depending on concentration, can produce superficial to medium (and in high strengths, deep) peels. At medium depth it does more in one session: improving texture, deeper pigmentation, fine lines and contributing to acne-scar treatment — an RCT combined microneedling with a 15% TCA peel and found significant improvement in atrophic acne scars. It's also used in a focused technique called TCA CROSS, where high-strength acid is applied precisely into individual ice-pick or boxcar scars rather than across the whole face.

But TCA carries the most caution on Indian skin. Because it can reach deeper and cause more inflammation, the risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and, at higher strengths, scarring is greater on darker skin, so medium TCA peels are used selectively, conservatively, and by experienced hands, with careful priming and aftercare. Deep TCA peeling is generally avoided altogether on Fitzpatrick IV–VI. TCA is a powerful, valuable tool for the right indication in the right hands, but it is not a casual first peel and not something to seek out based on strength alone — the stronger the peel, the more the operator's skill and your skin's tolerance matter.

sections.heading: How a Clinician Actually Chooses
sections.html:
Putting it together, here's the logic behind the recommendation you'll get:

  • Oily, congested, acne-prone skin / blackheads: salicylic acid (BHA), sometimes salicylic-mandelic blends.
  • Dull, uneven texture, fine lines, epidermal pigmentation: glycolic acid (AHA).
  • Deep-toned, sensitive, reactive skin, melasma, first-timers: mandelic acid (or gentle blends) to minimise pigmentation risk.
  • Texture, deeper pigment, individual scars, more in one session: TCA, used cautiously and often in combination (e.g. with microneedling) or focally (CROSS).
  • Mixed concerns: blended 'combination' peels or alternating agents across a course.

Layered on top of this is your skin tone and history: on Indian skin the clinician weights every choice toward minimising inflammation and pigmentation, which often means starting gentler and building up. This is why 'which peel is best' has no universal answer and why a peel recommendation is a clinical judgement — the acid, strength, contact time and number of sessions are all tuned to you, not pulled off a fixed menu.

sections.heading: Choosing Well on Indian Skin
sections.html:
Two principles should guide any peel choice on Fitzpatrick IV–VI skin. First, gentler and repeated beats strong and aggressive. Darker skin gets excellent results from a course of well-chosen superficial peels, and the main thing that derails those results is over-treatment triggering pigmentation. So an experienced clinician will often choose mandelic or carefully-dosed glycolic/salicylic, prime the skin beforehand, and build strength across sessions rather than going hard early. Second, sun protection is part of the peel. Whichever acid you choose, unprotected sun before, during or after undoes the benefit and raises the pigmentation risk — on Indian skin, daily broad-spectrum sunscreen isn't optional, it's the foundation the whole peel depends on, and it independently improves tone.

It's also worth being clear that at-home 'peel' products and the strong professional peels discussed here are different leagues — home acids are far milder, and the dramatic in-clinic peels should only be done professionally, because strength, neutralisation and reading your skin's reaction all require training, particularly on darker tones. If you're choosing a peel, the most useful thing you can do isn't to pick the acid yourself — it's to get your skin and concern assessed so the right acid, at the right strength, is matched to you. Book a free consultation and we'll recommend the peel that fits your skin, or see our chemical peel page for the full picture.

It's also worth remembering that a peel rarely works in isolation — it's most effective layered onto a sensible daily routine. Whichever acid you have in clinic, supporting it at home with a gentle cleanser, a suitable active (a mild AHA or a BHA cleanser for oily skin, used as directed), good moisturisation and daily sunscreen is what sustains the result between sessions and after the course ends. Many people also benefit from alternating concerns over time — a few salicylic peels while acne is active, then shifting to glycolic or mandelic for tone and texture once it's controlled — rather than committing to one acid forever. Skin changes with the seasons, with hormones and with age, so the 'right' peel for you this year may not be the one you need next year. That's another reason the most useful thing is an ongoing relationship with a clinician who knows your skin, rather than a one-off choice of acid. Think of the acid names not as competing products to pick a winner from, but as a toolkit your clinician draws on — reaching for salicylic when you're congested, glycolic or mandelic when you want brightness and even tone, and TCA selectively when depth is needed — adjusting the choice as your skin and your goals change over the months and years.

faqs.q: What is the difference between salicylic and glycolic peels?
faqs.a: Salicylic acid is a BHA that is oil-soluble, so it penetrates pores and suits oily, acne-prone and congested skin. Glycolic acid is an AHA that is water-soluble and works on the surface, so it suits dullness, texture, fine lines and epidermal pigmentation.

faqs.q: Which peel is best for oily, acne-prone skin?
faqs.a: Salicylic acid, because it is oil-soluble, penetrates and clears pores, and is anti-inflammatory. A trial found 30% salicylic acid peels significantly improved moderate-to-severe acne.

faqs.q: Which peel is safest for dark Indian skin?
faqs.a: Mandelic acid is often preferred for darker and sensitive skin because its large molecule penetrates slowly, causing less irritation and a lower risk of post-inflammatory pigmentation, while still brightening and helping pigmentation and mild acne. Carefully-dosed glycolic and salicylic are also used.

faqs.q: Is a TCA peel better because it's stronger?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. TCA can go deeper and do more in one session, but on Indian skin it carries a higher risk of pigmentation and scarring, so it is used cautiously and selectively. Stronger isn't safer — the right peel is the one matched to your concern and skin tone.
